summary: Describes 6rd, which lets a service provider rapidly deploy IPv6 to IPv4 customer sites. It builds on 6to4 and uses stateless IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation to cross IPv4-only infrastructure. It is informational.

eli5.summary: An internet provider can give customers the new addressing over its old network by wrapping new packets in old-style envelopes. This note describes how to do it quickly.

questions: how do isps deploy ipv6 over ipv4
can 6rd work with private ipv4 addresses
subtitle: How ISPs rapidly deploy IPv6 over existing IPv4 networks to customers

tldr.problem: ISPs have existing IPv4 infrastructure reaching customers but want to offer IPv6 without major investment, yet standard 6to4 does not provide reliable full IPv6 connectivity.
tldr.mechanism: 6rd modifies 6to4 by replacing the standard 6to4 prefix with the ISP's own IPv6 prefix and operating gateways at the ISP boundary to ensure all traffic destined for the ISP's 6rd customers traverses the ISP's relays.
tldr.outcome: ISPs can rapidly deploy native-looking IPv6 to customers using stateless encapsulation over existing IPv4 infrastructure, with a real-world example of over 1.5 million sites deployed in five weeks.

facts.label: Required relay gateways
facts.value: One or more at ISP boundary

today: RFC 5569 is an Informational document that remains active and relevant. While 6to4 has been deprecated (RFC 7526, June 2015), 6rd has been more stable and continues to be used by some ISPs as a transition mechanism toward native IPv6 deployment.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
IPv4 addresses are becoming scarce, and upgrading to IPv6 requires investment. However, many Internet Service Providers already have equipment at customer sites (Customer Premise Equipment, or CPE) with routing capability, and they have IPv6 address space allocated by their regional registry. The challenge is deploying IPv6 rapidly without requiring major changes to the existing IPv4 infrastructure or imposing costs on customers.

The RFC demonstrates a real-world solution: a major French ISP deployed 6rd in just five weeks and enabled IPv6 for more than 1.5 million residential customers. The approach builds on the existing 6to4 mechanism but modifies it so that the ISP uses its own IPv6 prefix instead of the standard 6to4 prefix, and operates relay gateways at its boundary with the IPv6 Internet to ensure reliable connectivity.
sections.eli5: An ISP can upgrade all its customers to the new address system in weeks without expensive hardware changes, just by tweaking an existing technique and running gateway machines at the edge of its network.

sections.title: How 6rd Works
sections.content:
6rd extends 6to4 by using the ISP's own IPv6 prefix instead of the standard 2002::/16 prefix. Each customer's IPv6 address is constructed by concatenating the ISP's IPv6 prefix with the customer's IPv4 address: the first part of the IPv6 address comes from the ISP's allocation (typically a /32 or shorter), and the remaining bits come from the customer's public IPv4 address. This creates a one-to-one mapping between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses without requiring a database lookup.

The ISP operates 6rd relay gateways at its border with the IPv6 Internet. These gateways receive IPv6 packets destined to the ISP's customers and encapsulate them in IPv4 packets directed to the appropriate customer IPv4 address. Customer CPEs perform the inverse: they recognize outgoing IPv6 traffic destined for other 6rd customers and encapsulate it, sending it to a relay gateway's IPv4 anycast address chosen by the ISP. This stateless, rule-based approach requires no per-customer state in the gateways.
sections.eli5: The customer's new address is built from the ISP's address prefix plus the customer's old IPv4 number. Gateways at the ISP edge wrap and unwrap packets so they travel through the old network.

sections.title: Addressing and Traffic Handling
sections.content:
Because the IPv6 prefix encodes the customer's IPv4 address, IPv6 communication between two customers of the same ISP is direct across the ISP's IPv4 infrastructure: each customer's CPE recognizes that the destination IPv6 address starts with its ISP's 6rd prefix, extracts the IPv4 destination from the encoded IPv6 address, and sends the encapsulated packet directly to that address. No relay is needed for intra-ISP traffic.

Traffic from the global IPv6 Internet destined for 6rd customers is guaranteed to enter the ISP's relay gateways because the ISP advertises routes for its 6rd prefix in the IPv6 Internet. The ISP's relays will only receive packets destined for their own customers, not for other ISPs' 6rd customers. This avoids the fundamental limitation of 6to4, where relays cannot guarantee they will reach the complete IPv4 Internet and may become overloaded with traffic from other 6to4 ISPs.
sections.eli5: Customers can talk to each other directly over the old network by encoding each other's address. Messages from outside go through the ISP's gateways so the ISP can manage them properly.

sections.title: Deployment and Variants
sections.content:
The RFC describes 6rd deployment in two scenarios. In the standard case, each customer receives a public IPv4 address, so the customer's IPv6 prefix is globally unique. Alternatively, if an ISP cannot provide global IPv4 addresses and instead uses private addresses (such as 10.x.x.x), the ISP can still use 6rd by operating NATs at the boundary and using the private address in the IPv6 prefix. In that case, the ISP may need to operate multiple 6rd domains if the number of customers exceeds what can fit in a single private address space.

The RFC notes that limiting the customer's IPv6 prefix to 32 bits of IPv4 address encoding initially restricted customers to one IPv6 subnet per site. However, once the ISP obtained a shorter prefix from the registry (moving from /32 to /26 in the real-world example), more subnets became possible simply by using different bits of the IPv6 prefix for different customer sites, without requiring changes to the gateways or CPEs.
sections.eli5: The approach works with private addresses too, and if an ISP grows and gets a bigger address block from the registry, customers automatically get more IPv6 subnets without any reconfiguration.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Spoofing
sections.content:
The RFC requires security checks at both CPEs and relay gateways. CPEs must validate that outgoing traffic has an IPv6 source address that is a valid 6rd address for the customer's site, and incoming traffic has an IPv6 source that matches the IPv4 source (derived from the IPv6 encoding). Relays must verify that incoming IPv6 traffic destined for the ISP's 6rd addresses comes from a valid IPv6 source outside the ISP's 6rd prefix, and that the destination is not a multicast address.

Despite these checks, if IPv4 address spoofing is possible in the underlying network, IPv6 address spoofing in 6rd is also possible because the IPv6 address is derived from the IPv4 address. The RFC notes that this is no worse than the underlying IPv4 security assumptions, and that network-level protections against IPv4 spoofing (such as ingress filtering) provide corresponding protection for 6rd.
sections.eli5: Gateways check that addresses match what they should be, but they depend on the underlying IPv4 network not allowing people to lie about where they are sending from.
